text:
## Observations

1. Each participant corresponds to a unique nonempty subset of the five problems, so there are \(2^5-1=31\) participants.
2. A participant’s name lists their selected problems in A–E order, and their score is the sum of those problems’ scores.
3. Participants rank by descending total score. When totals tie, their names rank in ordinary lexicographic order, with a shorter name coming first if it is a prefix of the other.
4. The output contains every participant’s name exactly once, one per line.

## Solution sketch

1. “Each participant corresponds to a unique nonempty subset of the five problems, so there are \(2^5-1=31\) participants.”

   Read the five scores and associate them with A through E in input order. Represent each subset by a five-bit mask, with one bit per problem. Enumerate masks 1 through 31 so that every participant is generated and the empty subset is skipped.

2. “A participant’s name lists their selected problems in A–E order, and their score is the sum of those problems’ scores.”

   For each mask, scan the problems from A through E. Whenever a problem’s bit is set, append its letter to the name and add its score to the total. Store the resulting name and total as one record. The same scan handles single-problem participants and the participant who solved all five.

3. “Participants rank by descending total score. When totals tie, their names rank in ordinary lexicographic order, with a shorter name coming first if it is a prefix of the other.”

   Sort the records in ascending order by negative total score, then by name. Negating the total places higher scores first, and ordinary string comparison resolves ties, including ties caused by equal problem scores or by different subsets with the same sum.

4. “The output contains every participant’s name exactly once, one per line.”

   Traverse the sorted records and print each name on its own line. With 31 records and names of at most five characters, the algorithm uses constant time and space under the stated constraints. For \(n\) problems and \(M=2^n-1\) participants, generation and output take \(O(nM)\) time, sorting takes \(O(nM\log M)\) worst-case time because a name comparison can inspect up to \(n\) characters, and storage takes \(O(nM)\) space.
